### The mechanism: an exact block-product identity

Fix n ≥ 1 and K ≥ 0. For each prime p define `j_p(n) := (−n) mod p ∈ [0, p−1]` (with j_p = 0 when p | n).

**Claim (Identity I).** For every n, K:
```
Σ_{j=0}^{K} v(n,j)  =  ω( ∏_{j=0}^{K} (n+j) ).
```
*Proof (both inclusions, exact, no normalization drift).*
(⊆) Let p | ∏_{j≤K}(n+j), so p | n+j for some j ≤ K. Then j ≡ j_p(n) (mod p) with j_p ∈ [0, p−1], hence j_p ≤ j ≤ K. Since j_p < p, the prime p is counted in v(n, j_p) (definition: prime factors of n+j_p exceeding j_p — and p > j_p holds by construction). So every prime on the right contributes ≥ 1 to the left sum.
(⊇) Conversely every term counted in v(n,j) is a prime p > j with p | n+j, j ≤ K, hence p | ∏_{j≤K}(n+j), and distinct primes contribute to distinct slots (each prime p divides n+j exactly for j ≡ j_p mod p; its slot j_p is the unique representative < p). Summing over j ≤ K counts each prime divisor of the product exactly once. ∎

**Immediate corollary (the family of lower bounds replacing R006's L1):**
```
v₀(n) ≥ ω( ∏_{j=0}^{K} (n+j) ) / (K+1)   for EVERY K ≥ 0.
```
Unlike `v₀ ≥ ω(n)` (the K=0 instance, killed in R006), this is a sup over K: divergence of v₀ is now *equivalent* to
```
sup_{K≥0}  #{ p ≤ n+K : (−n) mod p ≤ K } / (K+1)  →  ∞,
```
because #{p : (−n mod p) ≤ K, p ≤ n+K} = ω(∏_{j≤K}(n+j)) (a prime p > K divides at most one factor; a prime p ≤ K always has its slot j_p ≤ K ≤ p−1). This reformulation is exact in both directions and preserves every quantifier of the frozen contract — no sampled-to-universal step, no v/V conflation, no argument-order issue (the identity is in the original v(n,k) variables).
